questions.q: A column of prices such as '$1,200.50' has dtype object. What happens if you call astype(float) on it directly?
options: pandas strips the dollar sign automatically
It raises a ValueError because the text cannot be converted to a float
It converts every value to NaN
It silently keeps the column as text
questions.explain: astype(float) is strict. Remove the $ and comma first, then convert, ideally with pd.to_numeric.

questions.q: What does pd.to_numeric(series, errors="coerce") do with a value like 'n/a'?
options: Converts it to NaN so the rest of the column can be converted
questions.explain: coerce turns unparseable values into NaN, which you can then handle as ordinary missing data.

questions.explain: NaT (not a time) appears when to_datetime with errors="coerce" cannot parse a value such as 'not recorded'.

questions.q: The text '03/05/2024' parsed with format="%d/%m/%Y" gives 2024-05-03. Which lesson takeaway does this illustrate?
options: Ambiguous date strings can parse successfully into the wrong date, so specify the format you know the source uses
to_datetime always guesses correctly if the year has four digits
questions.explain: Both formats succeed on this string but give different dates. Only knowledge of the source's convention tells you which is right.

questions.q: Which is the best first step when you load an unfamiliar dataset and want to catch type problems?
options: Run df.dtypes or df.info() and look for numeric-looking columns stored as object
questions.explain: dtypes and info() reveal columns that pandas read as text because of stray symbols or values, before those columns break your calculations.
